summary: Google's answer to putting content in a real place is two things that share a name and not much else. ARCore is the phone half, delivered as a Google Play service and at version 1.56.0: it finds planes and depth from the camera, estimates lighting, reads printed images, and through the Geospatial interface recovers where the device is on the Earth by matching camera pixels against a point cloud built from more than fifteen years of Street View, so content can be pinned by latitude, longitude and altitude nearly anywhere Street View has been, and shared between people and between Android and Apple devices with Cloud Anchors that expire. Android XR is the headset and glasses half: an Android platform shipping on a Samsung headset while its software kit is still at Developer Preview 4, with perception built on OpenXR 1.1 and a long list of Google extensions, glTF 2.0 as the only content format, spatial and ambisonic audio, hands and eyes as the default input, and Gemini built into the system. The two halves are not the same product: visual positioning, Earth-referenced anchors and cross-device shared anchors exist only on phones, and on the headset an anchor persists to the app's own private storage and can be shared only with other applications running on that same device. Everything moves one way. The platform reads glTF, OpenEXR skyboxes and stereoscopic video and writes none of them; the only file it produces is a recording of a session as an ordinary video file with extra tracks. Two traps matter for a standards audience. ARCore's world coordinates are valid only inside the frame that produced them, because the world is refitted as tracking improves, so an anchor — not a coordinate — is the only durable address for a place. And the Earth-referenced pose is expressed in Google's own east-up-south frame with altitude above the 1984 world geodetic ellipsoid, with no exchange encoding of any kind, so every crossing into another system is a conversion someone has to write by hand. Conformance is split the same way: Android XR is listed by Khronos as a conformant OpenXR product, while ARCore's device certification requirements are only available to authorized manufacturers behind a portal.

coverage.note: The pixel pipeline is split and neither half is the platform's own for app content. ARCore on a phone rasterizes nothing: it hands the app a camera image and poses and the app draws. On Android XR the Jetpack XR runtime does rasterize, but only the fixed path it defines for glTF models, panels and skyboxes; anything else goes through OpenXR, where the app renders into its own swapchains and the system compositor only composes the layers. There is no render graph or pass structure a developer can configure.
